title: NASA closes Goddard research library amid campus consolidation
description_medium: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center closed its 100,000-volume research library in Greenbelt, Maryland, on January 2, 2026. The collection included books, journals, and historical documents, many not digitized or available elsewhere. NASA said it would review the holdings over 60 days, storing some and disposing of others. The library shutdown was part of a broader Goddard campus consolidation that also covered buildings and laboratories; it did not mean the center itself closed.
description_long: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, shut its research library on January 2, 2026. The roughly 100,000-volume collection held books, journals, and historical records, including material that was not digitized or available elsewhere. NASA spokesperson Jacob Richmond said the agency would review the holdings over the next 60 days, place some items in a government warehouse, and dispose of the rest under federal property procedures. Employees could still request research help through a digital “Ask a Librarian” service or borrow materials through interlibrary loan, but outside researchers lost in-person access to the collection. The library closure was part of a larger campus consolidation plan that NASA said included closing 13 buildings and more than 100 science and engineering laboratories by March 2026. The agency described the changes as consolidation rather than closure of Goddard itself and said the facility plan predated the Trump administration, while employees and union representatives disputed how the changes were being carried out. The defensible event is the library’s shutdown and resulting access and collection changes.
evidence_notes: New York Times reporting updated Jan. 2, 2026 describes the library's Jan. 2 shutdown, 100,000-volume collection, 60-day holdings review, planned storage/disposal, interlibrary access alternatives, and Goddard campus consolidation; NASA's spokesperson distinguished consolidation from closing the center.
corrected_wording: Specify that Goddard's research library closed; the broader campus plan involved building/lab consolidation, not closure of the entire center.

title: CDC shifts six childhood vaccine groups to shared decision-making
description_medium: On January 5, 2026, Acting CDC Director Jim O’Neill accepted a federal assessment and changed the childhood immunization schedule into three recommendation categories. Six vaccine groups—rotavirus, COVID-19, influenza, meningococcal disease, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B—were assigned to shared clinical decision-making. They were not simply removed for adolescents: rotavirus vaccination is for infants, and recommendations remain age- and risk-specific. CDC said all vaccines would remain covered without cost-sharing. A later court order stayed the January schedule revision.
description_long: On January 5, 2026, Deputy HHS Secretary Jim O’Neill, acting as CDC director, signed a decision memorandum revising the childhood immunization schedule after President Trump directed a review of other countries’ schedules. The new framework divided vaccines into those recommended for all children, those recommended for certain high-risk groups, and those based on shared clinical decision-making. HHS placed six vaccine groups—rotavirus, COVID-19, influenza, meningococcal disease, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B—in the shared-decision category. That was a change in recommendation category, not a blanket removal of six shots for ages 11–17; rotavirus, for example, is administered to infants, and recommendations depend on age and risk. HHS said all vaccines would remain covered by insurance without cost-sharing. The change followed a political directive and an assessment of international schedules, while HHS stated that access would continue. Its legal status later changed: CDC’s current provider schedule notes that a federal court stayed the January 5 memo and identifies the July 2025 schedule as the current schedule. The January action should therefore be described as a dated policy revision, not current guidance.
evidence_notes: CDC Jan. 5 release describes the decision memo, three categories, all-vaccine coverage, and follow-up implementation. HHS fact sheet lists the six shared-decision groups. CDC's current schedule page states a federal court stayed the Jan. 5 memo and the July 2025 schedule is current.
corrected_wording: Replace the claim that CDC stopped recommending six vaccines for ages 11–17 with the accurate category change; note that the schedule memo was later stayed by a court.

title: Misconduct complaint reported against Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer
description_medium: On January 9, 2026, the New York Post reported that a complaint to the Labor Department inspector general accused Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer of misconduct, including an alleged relationship with a subordinate and use of government resources for personal purposes. The claims were allegations at that stage. A later Labor Department inspector general report found policy violations involving official travel, alcohol on federal property, and staff assigned personal tasks, and described a relationship with a senior security agent as inappropriate and unprofessional.
description_long: On January 9, 2026, the New York Post reported that a formal complaint had been filed with the Labor Department’s Office of Inspector General concerning Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and senior aides. The complaint alleged an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, alcohol use during work hours, and improper mixing of official travel with personal activity; those claims were not established simply by the report of an inquiry. The Washington Post later reported that two aides had been placed on leave and that the secretary and department denied or declined to comment on the allegations. The inspector general’s final report, released in September 2026, subsequently found policy violations based on interviews and documentary evidence: Chavez-DeRemer combined official and personal travel without required approvals, regularly consumed and stored alcohol on department premises without written authorization, and directed employees to perform personal tasks during work hours. It also characterized her relationship with a senior member of her security detail as inappropriately close and unprofessional. The report’s administrative findings give the episode a documented outcome, but the record should not turn every initial allegation, including the word “affair,” into an established fact.
evidence_notes: The Jan. 9 New York Post report is the dated report of the complaint; Washington Post documents the administration's response and the aides' leave. DOL OIG's Sept. 3 final report documents administrative findings; AP independently summarizes the report.
corrected_wording: Describe the January account as allegations in an inspector-general complaint; use the OIG's later findings and precise wording rather than calling the reported relationship an established affair.

title: FBI searches Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s home
description_medium: On January 14, 2026, FBI agents searched Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s Virginia home under a warrant in an investigation of government contractor Aurelio Perez-Lugones, who was accused of retaining classified material. Agents seized Natanson’s phone, two laptops, and a smartwatch; the newspaper also received a subpoena seeking communications with the contractor. Authorities told Natanson she was not the target, and she was not accused of wrongdoing. President Trump was not shown to have directed the search.
description_long: The FBI executed a search warrant at Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s Virginia home on January 14, 2026, as part of a federal investigation into Aurelio Perez-Lugones, a Maryland-based government contractor accused of unlawfully retaining classified national-defense information. Agents searched Natanson’s home and devices, seizing her phone, two laptops—including a Post-issued computer—and a smartwatch. The newspaper separately received a subpoena seeking communications between Perez-Lugones and other Post employees. Investigators told Natanson she was not the focus of the probe, and she was not charged or accused of a crime. The warrant and the government’s statements concerned the contractor’s access to and retention of classified material; the criminal complaint against him did not accuse him of leaking the material he allegedly took. Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly defended the search as part of an effort to stop illegal leaks, while the Post called the action aggressive and raised press-freedom concerns. The record supports a search conducted by the FBI during the Trump administration, but does not establish that Trump personally ordered it.
evidence_notes: The Washington Post's Jan. 14 report identifies the warrant's target, devices seized, separate subpoena, investigators' statement that Natanson was not the focus, the charge against Perez-Lugones, Bondi's public statement, and the Post's press-freedom concerns.
corrected_wording: Use “FBI searches” and identify the contractor-focused warrant; remove any implication that Trump personally ordered the search.

title: Trump names Tom Homan to oversee Minneapolis operation as Bovino’s role shifts
description_medium: On January 26, 2026, after federal agents fatally shot Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, President Trump said he was sending border czar Tom Homan to oversee the administration’s immigration operation there. A senior official confirmed Homan would replace Gregory Bovino, who was expected to leave Minnesota. Reuters reported that sources described Bovino as demoted, while DHS publicly disputed that he had been relieved of duty. Trump also spoke with Governor Tim Walz and Mayor Jacob Frey about de-escalation and the federal presence.
description_long: On January 26, 2026, President Donald Trump said he was sending border czar Tom Homan to Minnesota to oversee Operation Metro Surge, the administration’s immigration-enforcement operation in the Minneapolis area. A senior administration official told Reuters that Homan would replace Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and that Bovino and some agents would leave the state. Sources told Reuters Bovino had lost his specially created “commander at large” title and would return to a California post, but the Department of Homeland Security disputed reports that he had been relieved of duty; the exact personnel action was therefore contested. The announcement came two days after federal agents fatally shot Alex Pretti, intensifying protests and political pressure. Trump also spoke by phone with Governor Tim Walz and Mayor Jacob Frey. Walz’s office said Trump would consider reducing the number of federal agents and allow Minnesota to investigate the shooting; Frey said some agents were expected to leave. The entry documents a proposed command change and attempted de-escalation, not proof that Homan had already arrived or that the dispute over Bovino’s status was resolved.
evidence_notes: Reuters, reporting Jan. 27 on events of Jan. 26, confirms Trump's Homan announcement, a senior official's replacement account, the conflicting Bovino personnel reports and DHS denial, the Pretti shooting, and calls with Walz and Frey. AP independently reports Bovino was expected to leave.
corrected_wording: Replace “deployed amid carnage” with an attribution that Trump said he was sending Homan; distinguish sources' demotion account from DHS's denial.
